intro: Good evening, and welcome to the What?? panel. Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honour all of them. Today's roll was seed 698833443. Here's every roll, and the play that came of it.

rolls.value: a bored lighthouse keeper · stacking · honey pots
rolls.became: Gannet Rock has a lamp to light at dusk and nothing else to do all day, so the keeper took up bees. Bees make far more honey than one keeper can eat, and a round tower has no shelves. So every jar goes on the spiral stair, one on top of another, up toward the lamp.

Every jar needs a label saying which flower its honey came from, written by hand. You type the label (CLOVER, GORSE, THYME) and the jar goes on the stair. Every letter is a jar, so long flowers are worth more.

Being bored, the keeper calls every label like a match over the lighthouse radio. "CLOVER! And it's ON the step!" Out in the dark, the fishing fleet has started listening, and by midsummer there's a fan club.

The supply boat. It comes at the end of every summer and takes the stair's honey to market, so there's always a clock in the corner of the scoreboard, and the boat on the horizon sails closer as it runs down.

Ottoline Vane, who kept Gannet Rock for thirty years before she retired to the mainland and a Sunday Sport radio show. Her record, a full stair, is scratched into the top step. She reviews every summer on air and does not think much of any of them.
Ottoline. She's in the corner of every review card, in her headset, with her bun.

rolls.value: a forced reset on a timer; runs grow longer as you learn
rolls.became: Summers. When the boat comes, the stair empties and the bees go back to nothing over winter. But Ottoline's reviews are oddly useful: every complaint is a Note, and Notes are what the keeper learns. Plant flowers that bloom later (sea thrift, bramble, rosebay, heather, ivy, Michaelmas daisies) and the next summer lasts longer, from 3½ minutes to almost 9.
Frames of bees fill jars on their own. Hives raise new frames. Queens, once you've learned to rear them, head new hives. By the late summers the rock is a monarchy.

So there isn't one. Jars are both the stair and the money, though: everything you trade with the boats comes off the stair. Spend early to stack faster, or stop spending and let the stair stand for the review.
The summer the stair reaches the top step, there's one jar left and one place it could go: the little shelf beside the lamp.

Put the jar on the lamp and the beam goes honey-gold for a night, and Ottoline gives it exactly one sentence on air. Or keep the lamp clear, finish one jar short, and the fleet comes home on a clean light and radios in that it was the best match all summer. Neither is a trophy. Ottoline's trophy, it turns out, is a plate.

About ten summers, each one longer than the last, over two or three sittings. Leave mid-summer and the boat waits for you (it won't sail without the commentary), while the bees keep filling jars, slowly.
Jars. A first summer is a few hundred, the middle summers are thousands, and Ottoline's full stair is a hundred thousand. Each step up the narrowing stair takes a taller stack.
The keeper's idea of summer, on a cold northern rock: a striped sun sinking into a neon grid sea, a candy-pink lighthouse, chrome-sunset lettering. The fonts are Monoton and VT323.
Eight colours, all of them: deep purple night, magenta and pink sky, an orange and yellow sun (and honey), blue and cyan sea.

A sunny calypso on steel drums in D dorian, as if a mainland station were coming through the radio. It gets busier in the last thirty seconds before the boat, goes quiet and slow over winter, and every typed letter ticks up the same scale.

rolls.value: an obscure observance on the release date
rolls.became: 4 November is Mischief Night in Yorkshire and the North, the eve of Bonfire Night, when children knock on doors and run. The harbour kids row out to Gannet Rock to do it. There's a sign for the door, among the Notes.

outro: That's the roll, folks. Back to the stair.
